title: CuO/ZnO/C electrocatalysts for CO2-to-C2+ products conversion with high yield_ On the effect of geometric structure and composition
abstract: The comprehensive application of electrochemical CO2 conversion to multi-carbon hydrocarbons and oxygenates is limited by the low selectivity and activity of copper-derived catalysts. Here, we report co-precipitated CuO/ZnO/C catalysts directing cascade catalysis to enhance the yield of the C2+ products. The reduced ZnO nanoparticles supply extra CO to increase the *CO surface coverage on the reduced CuO nanoparticles, which boosts the CeC coupling reaction kinetics on the reduced CuO surface. The geometric arrangement and composition of phase-separated CuO and ZnO nanoparticles are two vital factors influencing the CO utilization efficiency. The optimum CuO/ZnO/C catalyst exhibits a maximum Faradic efficiency of 74.0 % for overall C2+ products and 50.9 % for C2H4 at -0.75 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode, at which the total current density reaches 367mA cm.

CuO/ZnO/C electrocatalysts for CO2-to-C2+ products conversion with high yield: On the effect of geometric structure and composition Zhengyuan Lia, Ram Manohar Yadavb,c, Linping Suna,d,*, Tianyu Zhanga, Jianfang Zhanga, Pulickel M. Keywords: CO2electro-reduction C2+ products Tandem catalysis Copper oxide/zinc oxide
A B S T R A C T
The comprehensive application of electrochemical CO2 conversion to multi-carbon hydrocarbons and oxygenates is limited by the low selectivity and activity of copper-derived catalysts. Here, we report co-precipitated CuO/ZnO/C catalysts directing cascade catalysis to enhance the yield of the C2+ products. The reduced ZnO nanoparticles supply extra CO to increase the *CO surface coverage on the reduced CuO nanoparticles, which boosts the CeC coupling reaction kinetics on the reduced CuO surface. The geometric arrangement and composition of phase-separated CuO and ZnO nanoparticles are two vital factors influencing the CO utilization efficiency. The optimum CuO/ZnO/C catalyst exhibits a maximum Faradic efficiency of 74.0 % for overall C2+ products and 50.9 % for C2H4 at -0.75 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode, at which the total current density reaches 367mA cm−2.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The industrial revolution over the past century and thus the massive use of fossil fuels in industry and conveyance instigate the carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions and global climate change. The capture and utilization of CO2 is the ultimate strategy to recycle CO2 and achieve a carbon neutral society. [1] Among various modus operandi, the electrochemical conversion of CO2 to value-added chemicals has received immense heed due to the fast-growing source of renewable electricity. [2] The electrochemical route is currently impeded by the scarcity of concurrently active, selective, and durable electrocatalysts [1]. Copper (Cu) is the unique catalyst capable of converting CO2 into various hydrocarbons and oxygenates, but the rather poor selectivity and yield towards high-value C2+ products, such as ethylene, ethanol, acetate, and n-propanol, etc., limits its industrial implementaion. [3–5]
The C2+ products are formed through reductive CeC coupling reaction using CO as the intermediate in the CO2 electro-reduction process. Both vibrational spectra [6–8] and kinetic models [9–11] suggest that the dimerization of two *CO to form *OCCO is the key step for C2+ generation, especially at the low overpotential condition. The adsorbed *OCCO on Cu surface is stabilized by water solvation and field effects together enabling facile dimerization. [10–13] The constant electrode
potential model reveals that the dimerization barrier is only 0.21 eV at 0 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) on Cu (100) in the presence of a continuum distribution of charge in the solvent [12]. Moreover, the coupling barrier tends to decrease as applied potential increases, which is close to zero (∼0.05 V) at a moderate potential of -0.5 V vs. RHE [12]. Although the coupling of *CO is thermodynamically favorable, the formation of C2+ products, especially at the low overpotential region, is kinetically limited by the relative low *CO surface coverage on Cu. [3,14] Therefore, increasing the surface coverage of *CO on Cu surface by levitating the partial pressure of CO is an effective approach to enhance the C2+ products generation. [15,16] This is evidenced by the fact that CO electro-reduction yields C2+ products at a rate of over 10 times faster than CO2 electro-reduction at the low overpotential range. [17,18]
To overcome the deficient CO supply on Cu during CO2 reduction towards C2+ products, co-catalysts have been introduced by many researchers to create an in-situ feedstock of mobile CO reactant. [19–21] Some bimetallic catalysts integrating Cu with a CO-generating metal (e.g., Ag, Au, and Zn) have demonstrated CO spillover effect leading to improved activity and selectivity for CeC coupled products. [16,22–33] For instance, the polycrystalline Cu foil decorated with Au nanoparticles (Au/Cu foil) exhibited high C2+ alcohols superior to that of Cu

foil alone. [16] The Au/Cu foil catalyst reduced the overpotential by 260mV for the production of alcohols with a higher rate at the same time. The improvements are attributed to a tandem catalysis mechanism, where additional CO transferring from Au increases the local CO concentration within the diffusion boundary layer, which in turn can lead to a higher surface coverage of *CO on Cu. Investigations of phase-separated, oxide-derived CuxZn catalysts [23] and Ag-Cu2O catalysts [24] showed enhancements in C2+ selectivity, particularly for ethanol, where a CO spillover mechanism was also proposed. Alternatively, Cu surface modification by organic molecules (e.g., N-arylpyridinium and polyaniline) is capable of stabilizing *CO intermediate, which rises CO partial pressure to facilitate CO dimerization rate on Cu. [34,35] In general, a higher partial pressure of CO near the surface of the Cu electrode, leading to a higher surface coverage of *CO on Cu, allows for facile CeC coupling.
In the tandem catalysis, the CO utilization efficiency determines the selectivity towards C2+ products since the additional CO is generated by the 2e− reduction process of CO2-to-CO over the supplementary catalyst to Cu. The CO utilization efficiency on the tandem catalysts should be higher than that on the Cu catalyst alone in order to achieve higher selectivity towards C2+ products. Compared to noble metals and organic molecules, ZnO as a supplementary catalyst for Cu is more environmental benign and affordable. Herein using the carbon supported phase-separated CuO and ZnO nanoparticles (CuO/ZnO/C) as a model catalyst, we investigated the effect of two critical factors, geometric structure and composition, on the CO utilization efficiency by simply tuning the precipitation sequence and precursor ratio. The geometric effect has a strong impact on the CO transport from the reduced ZnO sites to reduced CuO surface, whereas the composition of two active sites modulates the balance of generation and consumption rate of CO intermediates.

sections.heading: 2.1. Chemicals
sections.text: Zinc nitrate hexahydrate (Zn(NO3)2·6H2O, 99 %), and sodium carbonate (Na2CO3, 99.5 %) were purchased from Alfa Aesar. Copper (II) nitrate trihydrate (Cu(NO3)2·3H2O, 99 %) was bought from Acros Organics. Carbon black (Vulcan XC72) was obtained from Cabot. All chemicals were used as received.

sections.heading: 2.2. Catalyst synthesis
sections.text:
The carbon supported CuO/ZnO catalysts were synthesized via a conventional co-precipitation method. In brief, 25mg of Vulcan XC72 was dispersed in 25mL of deionized water under sonication for 10min. 89mg (0.3mmol) of Zn(NO3)2·6H2O and 169mg (0.7mmol) of Cu (NO3)2·3H2O were added simultaneously at 60 °C. Na2CO3 as the precipitant was dropped wisely to the dispersion within 10min. The product was subsequently aged for 6 h under vigorous stirring followed by centrifugation and washing with deionized water several times. The precipitate was dried at 80 °C overnight and calcined at 330 °C in air for 1 h. The obtained samples were labeled as 7CuO/3ZnO/C in which the corresponding molar ratio of Cu : Zn was 7 : 3. The control sample was prepared without adding Zn(NO3)2, and denoted as CuO/C. Additionally, two more samples with different molar ratios of Cu : Zn (8 : 2 and 9 : 1) were prepared and labeled as 8CuO/2ZnO/C and 9CuO/ 1ZnO/C, respectively.
To investigate the effect of geometric structure on the catalytic performance, two extra samples were prepared via sequential precipitation method. The molar ratio of Cu : Zn was fixed at 7 : 3. Cu (NO3)2 was initially dissolved in carbon dispersion. When the precipitation between Cu(NO3)2 and Na2CO3 was completed, Zn(NO3)2 was added into the solution. After aging and calcining, the obtained sample was labeled as CuO-ZnO/C. In contrast, during the preparation
process of ZnO-CuO/C, Zn(NO3)2, Na2CO3, and Cu(NO3)2 were added in sequence and followed the rest of the procedure as above.

sections.heading: 2.3. Materials characterization
sections.text: X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were collected by Rigaku D/Max Ultima II powder diffractometer equipped with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5406 nm). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was measured with PHI Quantera XPS spectrometer. Raman spectra were recorded via Renishaw’s inVia Raman microscope using a laser with a wavelength of 532 nm. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images were taken by FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope. The scanning transmission electron microscope equipped with EDS (STEM-EDS) was used to take high-angle annular dark-field STEM (HAADF-STEM) images and STEM-EDS mapping. Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES, PerkinElmer Optima 8000) was applied to determine the contents of Cu and Zn.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical measurements
sections.text:
The electrocatalytic performances of all catalysts towards CO2 reduction were tested in a customized flow cell with a fixed 1 cm2 electrode geometric area. Catalyst was airbrushed on a gas diffusion layer (GDL, Sigracet 39 BC) to form the cathode electrode. The prepared electrode was dried at 130 °C under vacuum for 1 h. The metal oxide catalyst loading was around 0.4 mg cm−2 based on the weight difference before and after the spray coating. A Ni foam was used as the anode electrode for oxygen evolution reaction (OER). FAA-3-PK-75 anion exchange membrane (Fuel Cell Store) was used to separate anodic and cathodic compartments.
The flow cell was run under ambient conditions. 1M KOH electrolyte was supplied to both cathode and anode sides by syringe pumps (New Era Pump Systems, Inc.) at 0.1 mL min−1. CO2 gas flowed through cathodic compartment at 15 sccm via a mass flow controller (Alicat Scientific). A potentiostat (Gamary Interface 1010E) applied a constant voltage to the flow cell and recorded the corresponding current. The cathode potential was measured relative to the Ag/AgCl (3M KCl) reference electrode. All potentials were converted to the RHE scale using: ERHE = EAg/AgCl + 0.209 V+0.0591 pH. An iR compensation was determined by potentiostatic electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measured at frequencies ranging from 0.1 Hz to 100 kHz. The long-term stability test was operated continuously under the potentiostatic mode at -0.75 V vs. RHE.

sections.heading: 2.5. Products quantification
sections.text: The gas products were monitored after 150 s of running by an online gas chromatograph (GC, SRI Instruments MultipleGas#5) equipped with both a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and a flame ionization detector (FID). Because of the large CO2 consumption under the high current density, we supplied Ar (10 sccm) to the outlet gas stream of the flow cell before looping to the GC. The Ar served as a reference gas to determine the real flow rate of CO2 in the outlet stream. The calibration curves were obtained from standard gas sample (PurityPlus Gases). The electrolyte after electrolysis was collected and analyzed by 1H NMR (Bruker AV 400MHz spectrometer) to quantify liquid products, in which 3-(Trimethylsilyl)propionic-2,2,3,3-d4 acid sodium salt (TSP) in D2O was used as an internal standard. Concentrations of different liquid products were calibrated by standard curves. The standard deviations were calculated based on the measurements of three independent electrodes. During the durability test, gas and liquid products were sampled with an interval of 0.5 h initially, 9 h in the middle period, and 3 h for the last 10 h running.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
The primary Cu and Zn based catalyst, CuO/ZnO/C (molar ratio of Cu : Zn= 7: 3), was synthesized by the classical co-precipitation on the carbon powder support. For comparison, two other classes of catalysts with the same Cu/Zn molar ratio were prepared by the sequential precipitation, CuO-ZnO/C (precipitation of Cu and Zn in sequence) and ZnO-CuO/C (precipitation of Zn followed by Cu). ICP-OES results revealed that the atomic ratios of Cu and Zn of these three samples are close to 7 : 3, in accordance with the ratios of precursors (Table S1).
The crystalline structures of three carbon supported CuO and ZnO catalysts were characterized by XRD measurements (Fig. 1a). The diffraction peaks of CuO dominate over these of ZnO because of the relatively larger weight percentage of CuO. The two strong peaks at 35.5 and 38.7°correspond to monoclinic CuO (-111) and (111) facets, respectively (JCPDS #48−1548). The denoted peaks at 31.8, 34.4, 36.2, 47.5, 56.6, and 62.9° are indexed to wurtzite ZnO (JCPDS #36−1451). The peak intensity of the ZnO component in ZnO-CuO/C is lower than that of the other two samples because CuO covers the ZnO surface resulting from the precipitation sequence. [36,37], All diffraction peaks show large full width at half maximum (FWHM), indicating the nanoscale size of both CuO and ZnO particles [38]. Raman spectra confirm the co-existence of CuO and ZnO on the carbon support (Fig. S1). Three peaks at 271, 320, and 602 cm−1 correspond to the A g, B g(1) and B g(2) modes of the CuO crystal, respectively. [39] A weak peak at 439 cm−1 belongs to the E2high mode of ZnO. [40] Typical carbon Dband and G-band peaks are located at 1352 and 1588 cm−1, respectively. [41]
The chemical states of Cu and Zn in the three catalysts above were analyzed by XPS. The high-resolution Cu 2p XPS spectra shows two peaks at 933.9 and 953.9 eV corresponding to the Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/ 2, respectively, for all three samples (Fig. 1b). In addition, there are two satellite peaks centered at about 943.0 and 962.6 eV, suggesting the
valence state of Cu2+ [42]. Cu LMM Auger spectra shows a peak at 917.5 eV (Fig. 1c), confirming that only Cu2+ exists at the surface of catalysts. [43] In Fig. 1d, the Zn 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 peaks can be found at 1022.3 and 1045.4 eV, respectively. The binding energy difference between these two peaks is 23.1 eV, which agrees with the reported value for ZnO. [42,44] The intact Cu 2p and Zn 2p binding energies for Cu2+ and Zn2+ states, respectively, suggest the negligible presence of electric effect between CuO and ZnO.
High-resolution TEM (HR-TEM) was performed to investigate the morphology and structure of CuO and ZnO. The metal oxide particles exhibit an ellipsoid or sphere-like shape in all three catalysts (Fig. 2). The particle sizes of CuO and ZnO are quite similar in three samples as well. In addition, the size of CuO nanoparticles approximates to that of ZnO nanoparticles. For example, in the CuO/ZnO/C sample, both CuO and ZnO nanoparticles have a particle size of 15−20 nm, in agreement with the XRD results. However, the EDS elemental mapping clearly shows that different precipitation sequences result in different spatial distributions of CuO and ZnO nanoparticles (Figs. 2 and S2). For the coprecipitation sample of CuO/ZnO/C, CuO and ZnO nanoparticles spread in an alternative arrangement. In other words, the ZnO (CuO) nanoparticles serve as spacers between the CuO (ZnO) nanoparticles, whereas the CuO (ZnO) nanoparticles surface is partially covered by ZnO (CuO) nanoparticles. For the CuO-ZnO/C sample, CuO nanoparticles are interconnected with each other while the interlocked ZnO nanoparticles stack on the top of CuO nanoparticles. Such an arrangement of metal oxide nanoparticles is caused by the precipitation sequence of CuO followed by ZnO. Similarly, for the ZnO-CuO/C sample, the CuO nanoparticles disperse on the surface of interconnected ZnO nanoparticles matrix. That is also attributed to the precipitation sequence of ZnO followed by CuO.
The activity and selectivity towards CO2 electro-reduction over CuO/ZnO/C and its counterparts, including CuO-ZnO/C, ZnO-CuO/C, and CuO/C were evaluated in a customized flow cell using 1M KOH
electrolyte under ambient conditions. All electrodes were maintained with the same loading of CuO. Eight products, including carbon monoxide (CO), methane (CH4), ethylene (C2H4), ethanol (CH3CH2OH), npropanol (CH3CH2CH2OH), acetate (CH3COO−), formate (HCOO−), and hydrogen (H2), were detected for all samples. The detailed product distribution for each catalyst was recorded in Fig. S3. For all four catalysts, the formation of CO dominates over hydrocarbons and oxygenates at the potentials more anodic than -0.62 V vs. RHE (Fig. 3). As the potential shifts negatively, the combined Faradic efficiencies (FEs) of C1 hydrocarbon (CH4) and C2+ products rapidly increase (Fig. S4), accompanied by a quick drop of the FE of CO. The potential-dependent tendency of production of CH4 and C2+ products aligns with that of CO consumption, indicating that CO is a key intermediate for these highorder products. [18,45]
Compared to bare CuO/C, incorporating ZnO into CuO improves the selectivity towards C2+ products, especially C2H4 (the dominant C2+ product), while suppressing the formation of CH4 (Fig. 3a–c). Among the three CuO and ZnO hybrid catalysts, CuO/ZnO/C shows the highest selectivity towards C2+ products as well as C2H4 at the potentials more negative than -0.62 V vs. RHE while the selectivity towards CH4 is the lowest. For example, the FE of C2+ increases from ∼49 % for CuO/C to 71.0 % for CuO/ZnO/C while the FE of CH4 decreases from ∼25 % for CuO/C to 0.3 % for CuO/ZnO/C at the similar potential (∼-0.74 V vs. RHE). The FE of C2H4 increases from ∼30 % for CuO/C to 45.5 % for CuO/ZnO/C at this potential. ZnO-CuO/C catalyst shows the second highest FEs of both C2+ products and C2H4, followed by CuO-ZnO/C at the negative potential range. Note that the FE of CH4 over ZnO-CuO/C is also higher than that on CuO-ZnO/C. Compared to CuO/C, the
introduction of ZnO also enhances CO2 reduction rate as reflected by the increased total current densities (jtotal) under the condition of comparable FE of H2, as shown in Fig. 3e. Specifically, CuO/ZnO/C reaches a high jtotal of 342mA cm−2 at -0.74 V vs. RHE at which the FE of C2+ products reaches the maximum, which is approximate 2.4 times higher than that of CuO/C. Correspondingly, the partial current density of C2+ and C2H4 is 245 and 156mA cm−2, respectively, for CuO/ZnO/ C. To investigate the effect of electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) on the electrocatalytic performance of various samples, the ECSA was estimated by the double-layer capacitance (Cdl) method. The normalized current densities of C2+ products also increased in the sequence of CuO/ZnO/C > ZnO-CuO/C > CuO-ZnO/C > CuO/C at the high overpentioal region (Fig. S5).
Operando X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) spectroscopy and Operando Raman spectroscopy have previously revealed that both CuO and ZnO were reduced to metallic states under CO2 reduction condition. [23,46] Our XRD analysis (Fig. S6) confirms that the spent CuO and ZnO are mainly in the form of Cu and Zn, respectively, although the dynamic oxide (Cu2O) surface cannot be excluded in our samples. [5,18] The reduced CuO is capable of reducing CO2 and CO to C1-C3 hydrocarbons and oxygenates, while the reduced ZnO is an excellent catalyst for CO2 to CO conversion. [3,4,47,48] A mechanism of tandem catalysis is proposed to rationalize the improvement of both FE and production rate of C2+ as well as C2H4 in the CuO and ZnO hybrid catalyst compared to CuO/C alone. [15,16,31,49] Spillover of CO produced on Zn sites to the Cu sites is feasible since CO weakly adsorbs on Zn sites (-0.07 to -0.20 eV) while it adsorbs on Cu sites with moderate binding strength (-0.40 to -0.76 eV) [50]. In the case of hybrid
catalysts involving CuO and ZnO, the extra supply of CO from Zn sites provides a micro-environment in which a higher local CO concentration exists at the Cu surface than that for CuO alone. The higher local concentration of CO contributes to the increase of the *CO surface coverage at the Cu surface, leading to enhanced reaction kinetics of CeC coupling between two neighbouring C1 species (e.g., *CO or CO reductive derivative such as *CHO) to form C2+ products. [3,11,24,26]
The efficiency of CO transport from Zn to Cu sites plays a vital role in determining the formation rate of C2+ versus CH4. The geometric arrangement of CuO and ZnO nanoparticles strongly influences the efficiency of CO transport in the tandem catalysts. According to the product selectivity, the alternating arrangement of phase-separated CuO and ZnO nanoparticles enables more efficient trapping of CO (generated from the Zn sites) at the Cu surface, which is in agreement with the previous observation. [51] Therefore, the selectivity shifts from the formation of CH4 to C2+ products in which C2H4 predominates for CuO/ZnO/C, compared to the CuO/C.
In contrast, both samples prepared by sequential precipitation, whose structures are featured by dispersion of CuO (ZnO) nanoparticles onto interconnected ZnO (CuO) nanoparticles matrix, are less efficient in delivering CO from Zn sites to Cu surface. Thus, on the Cu surface with a relatively low *CO surface coverage, a large percent of *CO is still further hydrogenated to form CH4 rather than being dimerized to form C2+ products. Notably, CuO-ZnO/C has lower CO utilization efficiency than ZnO-CuO/C as indicated by the lower combined FE of C1 hydrocarbon and C2+ products, whereas higher FE of CO at the studied potential range of -0.54 to -0.90 V vs. RHE (Figs. 3d and S4).
Another vital factor that influences the selectivity towards C2+ products is the composition in CuO/ZnO/C. An optimal composition should balance the total CO generation rate with the CO dimerization rate on Cu sites in order to achieve the maximum FE of C2+ products. Note that CO is generated on both Zn and Cu sites. In addition to CuO : ZnO molar ratio of 7 : 3 (referred to 7CuO/3ZnO/C), two additional coprecipitation samples with molar ratios of 8 : 2 and 9 : 1 were synthesized and denoted as 8CuO/2ZnO/C and 9CuO/1ZnO/C, respectively. The contents of Cu and Zn were further confirmed by ICP-OES
(Table S1). The XRD, XPS, and HR-TEM results show that crystalline structure, morphology, chemical state, and geometric distribution of CuO and ZnO nanoparticles of 8CuO/2ZnO/C and 9CuO/1ZnO/C resembled those of 7CuO/3ZnO/C (Figs. S7 and S8). At the low overpotential region (-0.42 to -0.61 V vs. RHE), the FEs of C2+ and C2H4 follow the order of 9CuO/1ZnO/C>8CuO/2ZnO/C>7CuO/3ZnO/C while the FE of CO observes a reverse order (Figs. 4 and S9). This order indicates that excess CO is supplied as the ZnO content increases at the low overpotential region so that CO cannot be coupled entirely on the reduced CuO sites. As the potential scans to the more cathodic value, the FE of CH4 increases as the ZnO content decreases (Fig. 4c). Specifically, for the 9CuO/1ZnO/C, the CH4 formation rate accelerates the most rapidly beyond -0.75 V vs. RHE, because of the least supply of CO to the Cu surface, which consequently leads to the dramatic decline of C2+ and C2H4 selectivity. Although the 8CuO/2ZnO/C has a little higher FE of CH4 than 7CuO/3ZnO/C at the potentials beyond -0.8 V vs. RHE, the 8CuO/2ZnO/C still exhibits slightly higher CO utilization efficiency for CeC coupling (Fig. 4a). The FE of C2+ reaches a maximum of 74.0 % while the FE of C2H4 reaches the peak value of 50.9 % at -0.75 V vs. RHE for 8CuO/2ZnO/C. Interestingly, the jtotal for the three co-precipitation catalysts is almost identical (Fig. 4e). The jtotal is achieved to 367mA cm−2 at -0.75 V vs. RHE for 8CuO/2ZnO/C. CuO/ ZnO/C samples with different compositions showed similar ECSA (Fig. S10). Therefore, the difference in ECSA is not the origin of difference in production efficiency and rate of C2+ products among our studied samples. In order to rule out the possible effect of Cu(I) species, we further doubled the amount of ZnO based on 8CuO/2ZnO/C, and labeled the sample as 8CuO/4ZnO/C. More areas of CuO/ZnO interface would be introduced leading to enhanced possibility of Cu(I) species stabilization. However, the selective and activity towards C2H4 and C2+ products decreased for 8CuO/4ZnO/C (Fig. S11), which can be attributed to less efficiency of CO utilization as discussed above. Therefore, tandem catalysis rather than the possible effect of Cu(I) is the main mechanism to influence the electrocatalytic performance. Compared to other reported Cu/Zn catalysts, our catalyst shows the best overall performance in terms of the FE and partial current density of C2+
products (Table S2). The 8CuO/2ZnO/C catalyst was also tested in the 1M KHCO3 electrolyte and exhibited C2H4 FE of 39.1 % and C2+ FE of 64.1 % at -1.07 V vs. RHE (Fig. S12). The C2+ formation rate drops in the neutral electrolyte due to the decrease of local pH compared to the basic one. [52,53],
The long-term durability test of 8CuO/2ZnO/C catalyst was performed in a continuous operation mode at the optimum potential of -0.75 V vs. RHE, where the highest FE of C2+ was achieved. As shown in Fig. 5, the jtotal oscillated slightly between 360–400mA cm−2 during the 75 h running. The FEs of C2+ and C2H4 were initially 72 % and 51 %, respectively. They were maintained above 67 % and 45 %, respectively, in the first 30 h. Afterward, the FE of C2H4 gradually degraded to 33 % at 75 h. Although the FE degraded progressively, the C2H4 production rate was still considerable because of the large current density.
The mechanism to the selectivity degradation is complicated in the flow cell. To the best of our knowledge, the degradation of selectivity is mainly attributed to the loss of hydrophobicity in the GDL rather than the catalyst degradation. [54,55] The “flooding” of the GDL prevents CO2 from transporting to the catalyst layer. Balance of hydrophobicity
and hydrophilicity in GDL and design of new cell configuration are desired for better water management to improve the durability of CO2 electro-reduction.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
We demonstrate a tandem catalyst based on carbon supported CuO/ ZnO for promoting CO2 electro-reduction towards overall C2+ products and C2H4. The reduced ZnO active sites continuously supply additional CO to neighbouring reduced CuO sites, which increases the *CO surface coverage at the reduced CuO sites, leading to the escalation of the CeC coupling reaction rate. The geometric arrangement of two distinct active sites plays a crucial role in determining the activity and selectivity. The alternating spatial arrangement of phase-separated CuO and ZnO nanoparticles facilitates the production of C2+ species owing to the more efficient transport of CO from the reduced ZnO to reduced CuO sites while suppressing the CH4 generation. The CuO/ZnO/C catalysts prepared through a conventional co-precipitation method allow us to tune the composition by simply varying the ratio of metal precursors. An optimal composition leads to the maximum FE of C2+ products via manipulating a balance between CO generation and dimerization rate. For the optimal 8CuO/2ZnO/C catalyst, the FEs of C2+ products and C2H4 reach a peak of 74.0 %, and 50.9 %, respectively, at -0.75 V vs. RHE, at which the jtotal achieves 367mA cm−2.
